title: Burgundy
summary: Burgundy from Chablis to the Mâconnais: how the hierarchy of regional, village, premier cru and grand cru works, and the villages and climats of the Côte de Nuits, Côte de Beaune, Côte Chalonnaise and Mâconnais.

lessons.title: The shape of Burgundy
lessons.intro: This lesson sets out the map of Bourgogne, the French name for Burgundy, its grapes, and the four-level hierarchy of appellations that runs through every later lesson.

p: Bourgogne runs from Chablis in the north-west to the Mâconnais in the south. Between them lie the Côte d'Or, split into the Côte de Nuits in the north and the Côte de Beaune in the south, and then the Côte Chalonnaise. Beaujolais lies further south and is studied as a separate region.
Each part has its own regional appellations, such as Bourgogne Côte d'Or and Bourgogne Côte Chalonnaise, which add a geographic name to the basic Bourgogne appellation.

The Côte d'Or is a narrow escarpment of roughly 50 km, running from just south of Dijon to the Maranges. The vines face east and south-east. Soils are limestone and marl from the Jurassic period, often mixed with clay.

The best sites usually sit at mid-slope, where drainage and sunlight are best. The top of the slope is cooler with thin soils near the woods. The flat land at the bottom has deeper, richer soils and is more prone to frost. Behind the Côte rise the cooler Hautes Côtes de Nuits and Hautes Côtes de Beaune.
The climate is continental, with cold winters. Spring frost, summer hail and rain at harvest are the main risks, so vintages vary a great deal.
Pinot Noir makes the red wines and Chardonnay the whites. Aligoté is the third grape, used for Bourgogne Aligoté and for Bouzeron, a village appellation for Aligoté only.

Gamay appears in Coteaux Bourguignons and in Bourgogne Passe-tout-grains, a red or rosé blend of Pinot Noir and Gamay. Saint-Bris in the Yonne is the one Burgundy appellation for Sauvignon. Crémant de Bourgogne is sparkling wine made by the traditional method.

The hierarchy has four levels. Regional appellations can come from anywhere in the region. Village appellations, also called communal, take the name of a village, such as Gevrey-Chambertin. Premier cru vineyards sit inside a village appellation. Grands crus are appellations in their own right.

A premier cru label shows the village, the words Premier Cru and usually the climat, as in Gevrey-Chambertin Premier Cru Clos Saint-Jacques. A wine blended from several premiers crus of one village is labelled with the village name and Premier Cru only. A grand cru label needs only the vineyard name, such as Chambertin.

There are 33 grands crus: 32 in the Côte d'Or and Chablis Grand Cru. In the 19th century many villages added the name of their most famous vineyard to their own. Gevrey became Gevrey-Chambertin in 1847.

A climat is a named, precisely bounded plot whose character has been recognised over centuries. The Climats of Burgundy were listed by UNESCO as World Heritage in 2015. A clos is a vineyard enclosed by a wall. A monopole is a vineyard owned by a single estate.

Monks shaped the map. The Cistercians of Cîteaux, founded in 1098, built the wall of the Clos de Vougeot. After the French Revolution church land was sold, and Napoleonic inheritance law split estates equally among children. Most vineyards now have many owners.

This explains the two kinds of producer. A domaine grows and bottles its own wine. A négociant buys grapes, must or wine and sells under its own name. The Hospices de Beaune, a charity hospital founded in 1443, holds a famous wine auction each November.

key: Bourgogne runs from Chablis to the Mâconnais; the Côte d'Or is split into Côte de Nuits (north) and Côte de Beaune (south).
The best Côte d'Or sites are usually mid-slope, on east and south-east facing Jurassic limestone and marl.
Four levels: regional, village, premier cru, grand cru. Grands crus are appellations in their own right.
33 grands crus: 32 in the Côte d'Or plus Chablis Grand Cru.
Pinot Noir and Chardonnay dominate; Aligoté has its own village appellation at Bouzeron.
Napoleonic inheritance law divided vineyards among many owners, which gave négociants their role.

questions.q: Which vineyard name did the village of Gevrey add to its own name in 1847?
questions.explain: Gevrey became Gevrey-Chambertin, borrowing the name of its most famous grand cru, as many Côte d'Or villages did in the 19th century.

questions.q: How is a wine blended from several premier cru vineyards of the same village labelled?
questions.explain: When several premiers crus of one village are blended, the label shows the village and Premier Cru without a climat name.

questions.q: Bouzeron is a village appellation for which single grape?
questions.explain: Bouzeron is the village appellation for Aligoté only.

questions.q: Where on the Côte d'Or slope do the best vineyards usually lie?
options: At the top, next to the woods
On the flat land at the foot of the slope
On the plateau behind the slope
questions.explain: Mid-slope sites combine good drainage and good sun exposure. The top is cooler and the foot has richer soils and more frost.

questions.q: What does the word clos mean on a Burgundy label?
options: A vineyard with a single owner
A cellar where the wine is aged
A vineyard enclosed by a wall
questions.explain: A clos is a walled vineyard, such as the Clos de Vougeot. A vineyard with a single owner is a monopole.

questions.q: Why do most Burgundy vineyards have many different owners?
options: Napoleonic inheritance law split estates among heirs
Phylloxera forced owners to sell small plots
INAO rules limit the size of each holding
The vineyards were divided by a classification in 1855
questions.explain: After the Revolution church land was sold, and inheritance law divided estates equally among children, fragmenting the vineyards.

questions.q: How many grands crus are there in Burgundy, counting Chablis Grand Cru as one?
questions.explain: There are 32 grands crus in the Côte d'Or, and Chablis Grand Cru makes 33.

questions.q: Which part of Bourgogne lies furthest to the north-west?
questions.explain: Bourgogne runs from Chablis in the north-west to the Mâconnais in the south.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four levels of the Burgundy hierarchy?
questions.explain: The four levels are regional, village, premier cru and grand cru. Cru classé belongs to the Bordeaux classifications.

questions.q: Why is the flat land at the foot of the Côte d'Or rated lower than mid-slope?
options: It is too steep to work
It may only be planted with Gamay
It has deeper, richer soils and more frost
questions.explain: The foot of the slope has richer soils and collects cold air, so it is more prone to frost. Mid-slope sites drain better and get more sun.

questions.q: In which year were the Climats of Burgundy listed as UNESCO World Heritage?
questions.explain: The Climats of Burgundy were listed in 2015. 1999 is the year of the Saint-Émilion listing.

questions.q: What is a négociant in Burgundy?
options: A grower who bottles only his own wine
A firm that buys grapes, must or wine and sells under its own name
An official who tastes wine for the appellation
questions.explain: A négociant buys grapes, must or wine and sells it under its own name. A domaine grows and bottles its own wine.

questions.q: Bourgogne Passe-tout-grains is a blend of which two grapes?
questions.explain: Passe-tout-grains is a red or rosé blend of Pinot Noir and Gamay.

questions.q: In which year was the Cistercian abbey of Cîteaux founded?
questions.explain: Cîteaux was founded in 1098. 1443 is the Hospices de Beaune and 1847 the renaming of Gevrey-Chambertin.

questions.q: Which best describes the climate of Burgundy?
questions.explain: Burgundy is continental, with cold winters, spring frost, summer hail and a risk of rain at harvest.

cards.f: Which two grapes make most Burgundy wine?
cards.b: Pinot Noir for the reds and Chardonnay for the whites.
Burgundy's third grape, a white variety used for Bourgogne Aligoté and for the village appellation Bouzeron.
A narrow escarpment of about 50 km from just south of Dijon to the Maranges, with vines facing east and south-east.

cards.f: What soils underlie the Côte d'Or?
cards.b: Limestone and marl from the Jurassic period, often mixed with clay.

cards.f: Why are mid-slope sites on the Côte d'Or usually the best?
cards.b: They combine good drainage with good sun. The top is cooler with thin soils, and the foot has richer soils and more frost.

cards.f: Hautes Côtes de Nuits and Hautes Côtes de Beaune
cards.b: Cooler regional areas in the hills behind the Côte d'Or.

cards.f: What are the main weather risks in Burgundy?
cards.b: Spring frost, summer hail and rain at harvest. The climate is continental, so vintages vary a great deal.

cards.f: What are the four levels of the Burgundy hierarchy?
cards.b: Regional, village (communal), premier cru and grand cru.

cards.f: How does a premier cru differ legally from a grand cru?
cards.b: A premier cru sits inside a village appellation. A grand cru is an appellation in its own right.

cards.f: How is a grand cru named on the label?
cards.b: By the vineyard name alone, such as Chambertin, without the village name.

cards.f: How many grands crus does Burgundy have?
cards.b: 33: 32 in the Côte d'Or plus Chablis Grand Cru.

cards.f: Why do many Côte d'Or villages have double names?
cards.b: In the 19th century they added the name of their most famous vineyard. Gevrey became Gevrey-Chambertin in 1847.
A named, precisely bounded vineyard plot whose character has been recognised over centuries.

cards.f: When were the Climats of Burgundy listed by UNESCO?
cards.b: In 2015, as World Heritage. The listing covers 1,247 climats on the slopes south of Dijon, with Dijon and Beaune.
A clos is a vineyard enclosed by a wall. A monopole is a vineyard owned by a single estate.
A domaine grows and bottles its own wine. A négociant buys grapes, must or wine and sells it under its own name.

cards.f: Why are most Burgundy vineyards split among many owners?
cards.b: Church land was sold after the Revolution, and Napoleonic inheritance law split estates equally among children.
Red or rosé from Pinot Noir and Gamay. Pinot Noir must be over 30% and Gamay over 15% of the vines.
Regional appellation created in 2011 in place of Bourgogne Grand Ordinaire. Reds may use Gamay and Pinot Noir.
Traditional method sparkling wine, at least 9 months on the lees. Éminent needs 24 months and Grand Éminent 36 months.

lessons.title: Chablis and the Grand Auxerrois
lessons.intro: This lesson covers Chablis, its Kimmeridgian soils and its four levels from Petit Chablis to Chablis Grand Cru, and the smaller appellations around Auxerre in the Yonne.

p: Chablis lies in the Yonne department, around the small town of Chablis on the Serein river. It is far north-west of the Côte d'Or and closer to the Aube vineyards of Champagne than to Beaune.

The climate is cool and continental. Chardonnay ripens here only just. Spring frost is the great threat. Growers protect the buds with heaters among the vines or with sprinklers that coat the buds in ice, which shields them from colder air.
The classic soil is Kimmeridgian: marl and limestone from the Upper Jurassic, full of the fossils of a small oyster, Exogyra virgula. The same layer appears in the Aube and in Sancerre.

Chablis, Chablis Premier Cru and Chablis Grand Cru come mainly from Kimmeridgian slopes. Petit Chablis comes mostly from the younger, harder Portlandian limestone on the plateaux. As the vineyard expanded from the 1970s, growers argued over whether Portlandian sites deserved the name Chablis.

sections.h: Four levels and the premiers crus
p: Chablis has four levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Chablis Premier Cru and Chablis Grand Cru. All are Chardonnay only. The wines are pale, with high acidity, green apple and citrus fruit, often described as flinty or saline. Most Petit Chablis and Chablis are made without new oak.

Premiers crus lie on both banks of the Serein. On the right bank are Fourchaume, Mont de Milieu and Montée de Tonnerre. On the left bank are Vaillons, Montmains and Côte de Léchet. Many smaller climats may be sold under the name of a larger, better known one.

Chablis Grand Cru is one appellation with seven climats: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir. They share a single hillside on the right bank of the Serein, facing south-west over the town.

Les Clos is the largest and often the most powerful, slow to open. La Moutonne is not an official climat but a monopole lying across Vaudésir and Preuses. Grand cru wines are richer and longer lived than other Chablis, and some producers age them in oak barrels.

Around Auxerre lie smaller appellations. Irancy is a village appellation for red wine from Pinot Noir, with a little César allowed. Saint-Bris makes white from Sauvignon Blanc and Sauvignon Gris, the only Sauvignon appellation in Burgundy. Vézelay makes white from Chardonnay.
Several regional Bourgogne names add a local place: Côtes d'Auxerre, Chitry, Coulanges-la-Vineuse, Epineuil and Tonnerre near the town of Tonnerre, and Côte Saint-Jacques near Joigny.

key: Chablis lies in the Yonne on the Serein river, closer to Champagne's Aube than to the Côte d'Or.
Kimmeridgian marl and limestone (Upper Jurassic, fossil oyster Exogyra virgula) underlie the best sites; Petit Chablis is mostly on Portlandian.
Four levels, all Chardonnay: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Chablis Premier Cru, Chablis Grand Cru.
Seven grand cru climats on one south-west facing slope on the right bank: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur, Vaudésir.
Spring frost is the main hazard, fought with heaters and water sprinklers.
Saint-Bris is Burgundy's only Sauvignon appellation; Irancy is red from Pinot Noir.

questions.q: On which river does the town of Chablis stand?
questions.explain: Chablis lies on the Serein, and its grand crus face the town from the right bank.

questions.q: From which geological period does Kimmeridgian marl and limestone come?
questions.explain: Kimmeridgian is an Upper Jurassic layer, rich in fossilised small oysters.

questions.q: Petit Chablis comes mostly from which soil?
questions.explain: Petit Chablis vineyards lie mainly on the younger, harder Portlandian limestone of the plateaux.

questions.q: How many climats make up the Chablis Grand Cru appellation?
questions.explain: Chablis Grand Cru has seven climats: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir.

questions.q: Where do the Chablis grands crus lie?
options: On one south-west facing slope on the right bank of the Serein
On the plateaux above the left bank
On flat land beside the river
questions.explain: All seven climats share a single hillside on the right bank, facing south-west over the town.

questions.q: Which is the largest Chablis grand cru climat?
questions.explain: Les Clos is the largest grand cru and often the most powerful.

questions.q: Which grape is the main variety of Saint-Bris?
questions.explain: Saint-Bris is the only Sauvignon appellation in Burgundy, made from Sauvignon Blanc and Sauvignon Gris.

questions.q: What is La Moutonne?
options: A monopole lying across Vaudésir and Preuses
A premier cru on the left bank
The eighth official grand cru climat
A red wine appellation near Auxerre
questions.explain: La Moutonne is not an official climat. It is a monopole that lies across the Vaudésir and Preuses grands crus.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a Chablis grand cru climat?
questions.explain: Fourchaume is a right bank premier cru. Valmur, Bougros and Preuses are grand cru climats.

questions.q: Which of these Chablis premiers crus lies on the left bank of the Serein?
questions.explain: Vaillons is on the left bank. Mont de Milieu, Fourchaume and Montée de Tonnerre are on the right bank.

questions.q: Which fossil is typical of Kimmeridgian marl?
questions.explain: Kimmeridgian marl is full of the fossils of a small oyster, Exogyra virgula.

questions.q: Why do some Chablis growers spray water on the vines on frosty spring nights?
options: The ice coating shields the buds from colder air
questions.explain: Water freezes on the buds, and the ice coat protects them from the colder air around it.

questions.q: Which red grape, besides Pinot Noir, may be used in Irancy?
questions.explain: Irancy is red from Pinot Noir, with a little César allowed.

questions.q: Chablis lies closer to which other wine region than to Beaune?
questions.explain: Chablis lies far north-west of the Côte d'Or and is closer to the Aube vineyards of Champagne.

questions.q: In which department does Chablis lie?
questions.explain: Chablis is in the Yonne, like Irancy, Saint-Bris and Vézelay.

questions.q: Which statement about Chablis Grand Cru is true?
options: It is one appellation covering seven climats
Each climat is a separate appellation
It lies on the left bank of the Serein
questions.explain: Chablis Grand Cru is a single appellation with seven climats on the right bank, all Chardonnay.

cards.b: Chardonnay. All four levels, from Petit Chablis to Chablis Grand Cru, are Chardonnay only.

cards.f: On which river does Chablis lie?
cards.b: The Serein, in the Yonne department.
Upper Jurassic marl and limestone full of the fossil oyster Exogyra virgula. It underlies Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru.

cards.f: Where else does the Kimmeridgian layer appear?
cards.b: In the Aube vineyards of Champagne and in Sancerre.
Younger, harder Jurassic limestone on the Chablis plateaux, where most Petit Chablis grows.

cards.f: What are the four levels of Chablis, from lowest to highest?
cards.b: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Chablis Premier Cru and Chablis Grand Cru.

cards.f: What is the main vineyard hazard in Chablis?
cards.b: Spring frost. Growers use heaters among the vines or sprinklers that coat the buds in protective ice.

cards.f: What is the typical style of Chablis?
cards.b: Pale, with high acidity and green apple and citrus fruit, often called flinty or saline. Most is made without new oak.

cards.f: How many grand cru climats does Chablis have?
cards.b: Seven, all inside the single Chablis Grand Cru appellation.

cards.f: Name the seven Chablis grand cru climats.
cards.b: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir.

cards.f: Where is the Chablis grand cru slope?
cards.b: A single hillside on the right bank of the Serein, facing south-west over the town.
The largest Chablis grand cru climat, often the most powerful and slow to open.
A monopole lying across Vaudésir and Preuses. It is not an official grand cru climat.

cards.f: Name three right bank Chablis premiers crus.
cards.b: Fourchaume, Mont de Milieu and Montée de Tonnerre.

cards.f: Name three left bank Chablis premiers crus.
cards.b: Vaillons, Montmains and Côte de Léchet.

cards.f: How many Chablis premier cru climats are there?
cards.b: 40 climats. Many smaller ones may be sold under the name of one of 17 main premiers crus.
Village appellation in the Yonne for red wine from Pinot Noir, with up to 10% César allowed.
Burgundy's only Sauvignon appellation: white wine from Sauvignon Blanc and Sauvignon Gris.
Appellation in the Yonne for white wine from Chardonnay.

cards.f: Which regional names add a local place in the Yonne?
cards.b: Bourgogne Côtes d'Auxerre, Chitry, Coulanges-la-Vineuse, Epineuil, Tonnerre and Côte Saint-Jacques.

lessons.title: The Côte de Nuits
lessons.intro: This lesson walks the Côte de Nuits village by village from Marsannay in the north to Nuits-Saint-Georges in the south, with the grands crus of each.

p: The Côte de Nuits runs from Marsannay, just south of Dijon, to Corgoloin. The slope is narrow and the wine is almost all red Pinot Noir. Of the 32 Côte d'Or grands crus, 24 lie here.

Marsannay is the only village appellation of the Côte d'Or for red, white and rosé. Fixin makes firm reds, with premiers crus such as Clos de la Perrière and Clos Napoléon. Côte de Nuits-Villages comes from the villages at either end: Fixin and Brochon in the north, Premeaux-Prissey, Comblanchien and Corgoloin in the south.

Gevrey-Chambertin is the largest village of the Côte de Nuits and has nine grands crus. Chambertin and Chambertin-Clos de Bèze are the most famous, and Clos de Bèze may also be sold as Chambertin. Most grands crus lie south of the village, towards Morey.

The others are Chapelle, Charmes, Griotte, Latricières, Mazis, Mazoyères and Ruchottes, each followed by -Chambertin. Mazoyères-Chambertin may be sold as Charmes-Chambertin. The premier cru Clos Saint-Jacques, on the slope north-west of the village, is often priced like a grand cru. Gevrey reds are powerful and structured, with dark fruit.

Morey-Saint-Denis has four grands crus of its own: Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis, Clos de Tart, a monopole, and Clos des Lambrays, raised to grand cru in 1981. A small part of Bonnes-Mares also lies in Morey.

Chambolle-Musigny has two grands crus. Bonnes-Mares lies at the northern end, next to Morey. Musigny lies at the southern end, next to the Clos de Vougeot, and is also known for a rare white wine. The premier cru Les Amoureuses sits just below Musigny. Chambolle reds are known for perfume and a silky texture.

The Clos de Vougeot is a walled grand cru of about 50 ha, built by the Cistercians. It runs from the upper slope down to the main road and is split among many owners, so quality depends on position and producer. Its château is home to the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin. Vougeot village wines include a white premier cru, Le Clos Blanc.

Vosne-Romanée has six grands crus. Romanée-Conti and La Tâche are monopoles of the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti. La Romanée and La Grande Rue are also monopoles, and La Grande Rue became grand cru in 1992. Richebourg and Romanée-Saint-Vivant complete the group.

Echezeaux and Grands-Echezeaux lie in the commune of Flagey-Echezeaux, whose village wine is sold as Vosne-Romanée. Leading premiers crus include Cros Parantoux, Les Suchots, Les Beaux Monts and Aux Malconsorts.

The town of Nuits-Saint-Georges gives the Côte de Nuits its name and is a centre for négociants. The appellation has no grands crus but many premiers crus. The most famous, Les Saint-Georges, Les Vaucrains and Les Cailles, lie south of the town.

The appellation continues into Premeaux-Prissey, with premiers crus such as Clos de la Maréchale, Clos Arlot and Clos des Forêts Saint-Georges. The reds are firm, dense and earthy, and need time in bottle.

key: The Côte de Nuits runs from Marsannay to Corgoloin and holds 24 of the 32 Côte d'Or grands crus, almost all red.
Marsannay is the only Côte d'Or village appellation for red, white and rosé.
Gevrey-Chambertin has nine grands crus; Clos de Bèze may be sold as Chambertin and Mazoyères as Charmes-Chambertin.
Morey-Saint-Denis: Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis, Clos de Tart, Clos des Lambrays (1981) and part of Bonnes-Mares.
Chambolle-Musigny: Musigny and Bonnes-Mares; Les Amoureuses is its most famous premier cru.
Vosne-Romanée has six grands crus; Echezeaux and Grands-Echezeaux lie in Flagey-Echezeaux. Nuits-Saint-Georges has none.

questions.q: What makes Marsannay unique among Côte d'Or village appellations?
options: It has the most grands crus
It covers red, white and rosé
It is for white wine only
questions.explain: Marsannay is the only village appellation of the Côte d'Or that includes rosé as well as red and white.

questions.q: Which Gevrey grand cru may be sold under the name Charmes-Chambertin?
questions.explain: Mazoyères-Chambertin may be labelled as Charmes-Chambertin, its neighbour.

questions.q: Which Morey-Saint-Denis vineyard was raised to grand cru in 1981?
questions.explain: Clos des Lambrays became a grand cru in 1981.

questions.q: Which famous premier cru lies just below Musigny in Chambolle-Musigny?
questions.explain: Les Amoureuses sits just below Musigny. The other three belong to Gevrey, Vosne and Nuits.

questions.q: In which commune do Echezeaux and Grands-Echezeaux lie?
questions.explain: Both lie in Flagey-Echezeaux, whose village wine is sold as Vosne-Romanée.

questions.q: How many grands crus does Nuits-Saint-Georges have?
questions.explain: Nuits-Saint-Georges has no grands crus, only many premiers crus such as Les Saint-Georges.

questions.q: Who built the wall around the Clos de Vougeot?
questions.explain: The Cistercians walled the Clos de Vougeot. Today it is divided among many owners.

questions.q: Which grand cru lies mainly in Chambolle-Musigny, with a small part in Morey-Saint-Denis?
questions.explain: Bonnes-Mares lies at the northern end of Chambolle, and a small part of it lies in Morey.

questions.q: How many grands crus does Gevrey-Chambertin have?
questions.explain: Gevrey has nine grands crus, more than any other village of the Côte de Nuits.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a grand cru of Vosne-Romanée?
questions.explain: Clos de la Roche is a grand cru of Morey-Saint-Denis.

questions.q: Which Vosne-Romanée vineyard became a grand cru in 1992?
questions.explain: La Grande Rue, a monopole, was raised to grand cru in 1992. Cros Parantoux and Les Suchots are premiers crus.

questions.q: Which village can contribute to Côte de Nuits-Villages?
questions.explain: Côte de Nuits-Villages comes from Fixin, Brochon, Premeaux-Prissey, Comblanchien and Corgoloin.

questions.q: Where do Gevrey-Chambertin's grands crus mostly lie?
options: North of the village, towards Fixin
South of the village, towards Morey
On the flat land east of the main road
In the Hautes Côtes behind the village
questions.explain: Most of Gevrey's grands crus lie south of the village, towards Morey-Saint-Denis.

questions.q: Roughly how large is the Clos de Vougeot?
questions.explain: The Clos de Vougeot covers about 50 ha, from the upper slope down to the main road.

questions.q: Which style is typical of Chambolle-Musigny reds?
questions.explain: Chambolle reds are known for perfume and silkiness. Firm, earthy reds are typical of Nuits-Saint-Georges.

cards.f: Where does the Côte de Nuits begin and end?
cards.b: From Marsannay, just south of Dijon, to Corgoloin.

cards.f: How many Côte d'Or grands crus lie in the Côte de Nuits?
cards.b: 24 of the 32, almost all red Pinot Noir.
The only Côte d'Or village appellation for red, white and rosé.
Wine from the villages at either end: Fixin and Brochon in the north, Premeaux-Prissey, Comblanchien and Corgoloin in the south.
Village known for firm reds, with premiers crus such as Clos de la Perrière and Clos Napoléon.

cards.f: How many grands crus does Gevrey-Chambertin have?
cards.b: Nine: Chambertin, Chambertin-Clos de Bèze, and Chapelle, Charmes, Griotte, Latricières, Mazis, Mazoyères and Ruchottes-Chambertin.
Gevrey grand cru that may also be sold as Chambertin.
Gevrey grand cru that may be sold as Charmes-Chambertin.
Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru on the slope north-west of the village, often priced like a grand cru.

cards.f: Which grands crus lie wholly in Morey-Saint-Denis?
cards.b: Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis, Clos de Tart (a monopole) and Clos des Lambrays. A small part of Bonnes-Mares is also in Morey.
Morey-Saint-Denis vineyard raised to grand cru in 1981.

cards.f: Which are the two grands crus of Chambolle-Musigny?
cards.b: Bonnes-Mares at the northern end, next to Morey, and Musigny at the southern end, next to the Clos de Vougeot.
Chambolle grand cru, the only Côte de Nuits grand cru that makes a white wine as well as red.
Chambolle-Musigny premier cru just below Musigny. Chambolle reds are known for perfume and a silky texture.
Walled grand cru of about 50 ha built by the Cistercians, now shared by many owners. Its château houses the Chevaliers du Tastevin.

cards.f: Name the six grands crus of Vosne-Romanée.
cards.b: Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, La Romanée, La Grande Rue, Richebourg and Romanée-Saint-Vivant.
Vosne-Romanée grand cru and monopole of about 0.85 ha, the smallest appellation in France.
Vosne-Romanée monopole that became a grand cru in 1992.
Grands crus in the commune of Flagey-Echezeaux, whose village wine is sold as Vosne-Romanée.
No grands crus but many premiers crus, such as Les Saint-Georges, Les Vaucrains and Les Cailles. Firm, dense, earthy reds.

lessons.title: The Côte de Beaune
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the Côte de Beaune from the hill of Corton to the Maranges: Beaune, the red villages of Pommard and Volnay, and the great white villages of Meursault, Puligny and Chassagne.

p: The Côte de Beaune starts at Ladoix-Serrigny. The slope is broader and gentler than in the Côte de Nuits, and much more white wine is made. The hill of Corton is shared by Ladoix, Aloxe-Corton and Pernand-Vergelesses.

Corton is the only red grand cru of the Côte de Beaune and the largest grand cru in Burgundy. Some white Corton is also made. The label may add a climat name, such as Le Clos du Roi, Les Bressandes, Les Renardes or Le Corton.
Corton-Charlemagne is the white grand cru, from Chardonnay on the upper part of the hill, named after the emperor Charlemagne. A separate Charlemagne appellation exists but is almost never used.

Savigny-lès-Beaune and Chorey-lès-Beaune make supple, fruity reds that are often good value. Beaune itself has no grands crus but a large area of premiers crus, including Les Grèves, Les Bressandes, Les Teurons, Clos du Roi and Le Clos des Mouches, which makes both red and white.

The town is the trading heart of Burgundy and home to many négociant houses. The Hospices de Beaune was founded in 1443 by Nicolas Rolin, chancellor to the Duke of Burgundy. Wine from its vineyards is sold at a charity auction each November.

Pommard and Volnay are both red-only village appellations with no grands crus. Pommard is sturdier and more tannic, with more clay in the soil. Its best premiers crus are Les Rugiens, named after its reddish, iron-rich soil, and Les Grands Epenots and Les Petits Epenots.

Volnay, next door, is lighter and more perfumed, on soils with more limestone. Leading premiers crus are Les Caillerets, Clos des Ducs, Taille Pieds and Clos des Chênes. Red wine from Santenots, which lies in Meursault, is usually sold as Volnay Premier Cru Santenots.
Up a side valley, Monthélie, Auxey-Duresses and Saint-Romain make lighter wines that often offer value.

Meursault is mostly white and has no grands crus. Its wines are rich and rounded, often with hazelnut and butter notes from barrel fermentation and lees ageing. The best premiers crus are Perrières, Genevrières and Charmes, with Les Gouttes d'Or and Le Porusot also well known.
The hamlet of Blagny sits above Meursault and Puligny. The Blagny appellation is for red wine. White wine from Blagny is sold as Meursault Premier Cru Blagny or as Puligny-Montrachet Premier Cru.

Montrachet straddles Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet. Chevalier-Montrachet lies above it on thinner, stonier soil, and Bâtard-Montrachet below it on deeper soil. Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet lies wholly in Puligny, Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet wholly in Chassagne.

Puligny has a high water table, so few cellars are dug deep. Its whites are precise and fine. Top premiers crus include Les Pucelles, Les Combettes, Les Folatières and Le Cailleret. Chassagne makes both white and red, with premiers crus such as Morgeot, Cailleret, La Romanée and Les Grandes Ruchottes.

Saint-Aubin, behind Puligny and Chassagne, is mostly white. Santenay and Maranges at the southern end are mostly red. Côte de Beaune-Villages is a red wine from the village appellations of the Côte de Beaune except Beaune, Aloxe-Corton, Pommard and Volnay.

key: Corton is the only red grand cru of the Côte de Beaune and the largest grand cru in Burgundy; Corton-Charlemagne is its white partner.
Beaune has no grands crus but many premiers crus; the Hospices de Beaune was founded in 1443.
Pommard and Volnay are red only: Pommard sturdier and more tannic, Volnay lighter and more perfumed.
Meursault has no grands crus; Perrières, Genevrières and Charmes are its leading premiers crus.
Five white grands crus around Montrachet: Montrachet and Bâtard shared, Chevalier and Bienvenues in Puligny, Criots in Chassagne.
Côte de Beaune-Villages is red and excludes Beaune, Aloxe-Corton, Pommard and Volnay.

questions.q: Which is the only red grand cru of the Côte de Beaune?
questions.explain: Corton is the only red grand cru of the Côte de Beaune. The others named are white.

questions.q: Red wine from the Santenots climat, which lies in Meursault, is usually sold under which name?
questions.explain: Red wine from Santenots is sold as Volnay Premier Cru Santenots.

questions.q: Which grand cru lies wholly within Chassagne-Montrachet?
questions.explain: Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet lies wholly in Chassagne. Montrachet is shared, and Chevalier and Bienvenues lie in Puligny.

questions.q: In which year was the Hospices de Beaune founded?
questions.explain: Nicolas Rolin founded the Hospices de Beaune in 1443.

questions.q: How do Pommard and Volnay usually differ in style?
options: Pommard is white and Volnay is red
Both are light and made for early drinking
Volnay is the more tannic of the two
Pommard is sturdier and more tannic, Volnay lighter and more perfumed
questions.explain: Pommard, with more clay, gives sturdier reds. Volnay, with more limestone, gives lighter, perfumed reds.

questions.q: Where does Chevalier-Montrachet lie in relation to Montrachet?
options: Above it, on thinner and stonier soil
Across the main road on flat land
questions.explain: Chevalier-Montrachet lies upslope from Montrachet on thin, stony soil. Bâtard-Montrachet lies below.

questions.q: Which of these villages cannot contribute to Côte de Beaune-Villages?
questions.explain: Côte de Beaune-Villages excludes Beaune, Aloxe-Corton, Pommard and Volnay.

questions.q: Which three villages share the hill of Corton?
questions.explain: The hill of Corton is shared by Ladoix-Serrigny, Aloxe-Corton and Pernand-Vergelesses.

questions.q: What is Corton-Charlemagne?
options: A red premier cru of Beaune
A village appellation for red and white
A blend of red and white grapes
The white grand cru on the upper part of the hill of Corton
questions.explain: Corton-Charlemagne is a white grand cru from Chardonnay on the upper slopes of the hill of Corton.

questions.q: Which of these is one of Meursault's leading premiers crus?
questions.explain: Genevrières is a top Meursault premier cru. Les Rugiens is in Pommard, Les Pucelles in Puligny and Le Clos des Mouches in Beaune.

questions.q: Under which name is white wine from the hamlet of Blagny sold?
options: Meursault Premier Cru Blagny or Puligny-Montrachet Premier Cru
questions.explain: The Blagny appellation is for red. White from Blagny is sold as Meursault Premier Cru Blagny or Puligny-Montrachet Premier Cru.

questions.q: Which of these grands crus lies wholly in Puligny-Montrachet?
questions.explain: Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet lies wholly in Puligny. Montrachet and Bâtard are shared, and Criots lies in Chassagne.

questions.q: Who founded the Hospices de Beaune?
options: Nicolas Rolin, chancellor to the Duke of Burgundy
questions.explain: Nicolas Rolin, chancellor to the Duke of Burgundy, founded the Hospices de Beaune in 1443.

questions.q: Why are Pommard reds usually sturdier than those of Volnay?
options: Pommard lies higher and is cooler
Volnay is aged without oak by law
questions.explain: Pommard has more clay in its soils and gives sturdier, more tannic reds. Volnay has more limestone.

questions.q: Which colour dominates in Saint-Aubin?
questions.explain: Saint-Aubin, behind Puligny and Chassagne, is mostly white. Santenay and Maranges are mostly red.

cards.f: Where does the Côte de Beaune begin and end?
cards.b: From Ladoix-Serrigny in the north to the Maranges in the south.

cards.f: How does the Côte de Beaune differ from the Côte de Nuits?
cards.b: The slope is broader and gentler, and much more white wine is made.
The only red grand cru of the Côte de Beaune and the largest grand cru in Burgundy. Some white is also made.

cards.f: Which three villages share the hill of Corton?
cards.b: Ladoix-Serrigny, Aloxe-Corton and Pernand-Vergelesses.

cards.f: Name some Corton climats that may appear on the label.
cards.b: Le Clos du Roi, Les Bressandes, Les Renardes and Le Corton.
White grand cru from Chardonnay on the upper part of the hill of Corton, named after the emperor Charlemagne.
Villages near Beaune making supple, fruity reds that are often good value.
Les Grèves, Les Bressandes, Les Teurons, Clos du Roi and Le Clos des Mouches, which makes red and white. Beaune has no grands crus.
Charity hospital founded in 1443 by Nicolas Rolin. Its wines are sold at an auction on the third weekend of November.
Red-only village with no grands crus. Sturdier and more tannic than Volnay, on soils with more clay.
Leading Pommard premier cru, named after its reddish, iron-rich soil.
Red-only village with no grands crus. Lighter and more perfumed than Pommard, on soils with more limestone.
Red wine from the Santenots climat, which lies in Meursault, usually sold under the Volnay name.
Mostly white, with no grands crus. Rich and rounded, often with hazelnut and butter notes from barrel fermentation and lees.

cards.f: Name the three leading premiers crus of Meursault.
cards.b: Perrières, Genevrières and Charmes.
Hamlet above Meursault and Puligny. Blagny AOC is red. Its white is sold as Meursault or Puligny-Montrachet Premier Cru.

cards.f: Name the five white grands crus around Montrachet.
cards.b: Montrachet, Chevalier-Montrachet, Bâtard-Montrachet, Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet and Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet.

cards.f: Why are few cellars dug deep in Puligny-Montrachet?
cards.b: The village has a high water table.
Makes both white and red. Premiers crus include Morgeot, Cailleret, La Romanée and Les Grandes Ruchottes.
Red wine from Côte de Beaune village appellations, except Beaune, Aloxe-Corton, Pommard and Volnay.

lessons.title: Côte Chalonnaise and Mâconnais
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the two southern parts of Burgundy: the five village appellations of the Côte Chalonnaise, and the Mâconnais with Pouilly-Fuissé and its premiers crus, created in 2020.

p: The Côte Chalonnaise lies south of the Maranges and takes its name from the town of Chalon-sur-Saône. Unlike the Côte d'Or it is not one continuous slope. The vineyards sit on scattered hillsides among other farmland.

There are no grands crus, but four of the five village appellations have premiers crus. Bouzeron has none. The wines are usually lighter and ready sooner than those of the Côte d'Or, and often good value. The regional appellations are Bourgogne Côte Chalonnaise and, to the west, Bourgogne Côtes du Couchois.

sections.h: Five villages from north to south
p: Bouzeron is the village appellation for Aligoté only. Rully makes more white than red and has a long history of sparkling wine production. Mercurey is the largest village and makes mainly red Pinot Noir.
Givry is also mainly red; tradition says it was a favourite of King Henri IV. Montagny, in the south, is for white wine from Chardonnay only, and a large part of it is classified as premier cru.

The Mâconnais lies further south, around the town of Mâcon on the Saône. It is warmer and sunnier than the Côte d'Or. Most of the wine is white Chardonnay, rounder and riper in fruit than wines further north. Reds are made mostly from Gamay. The village of Chardonnay lies here.

The base appellation is Mâcon. Mâcon followed by a village name, such as Mâcon Davayé or Mâcon Chardonnay, is a step up. Mâcon-Villages is for white wine only. Viré-Clessé and Saint-Véran are village appellations for white wine.

Pouilly-Fuissé lies in the south of the Mâconnais, below the limestone outcrops of the Roche de Solutré and the Roche de Vergisson. It covers four communes: Chaintré, Fuissé, Solutré-Pouilly and Vergisson. It is white only, from Chardonnay, and has more weight and structure than most Mâcon, often with oak ageing.
Its neighbours Pouilly-Loché and Pouilly-Vinzelles make similar whites in smaller amounts.

In 2020 Pouilly-Fuissé gained 22 premiers crus, from the 2020 vintage. They were the first premiers crus of the Mâconnais. Among them are Le Clos de Monsieur Noly, Les Crays, Vers Cras, Sur la Roche, Les Perrières, Le Clos Reyssier and Aux Quarts.
The label shows Pouilly-Fuissé Premier Cru with the climat name. Pouilly-Loché and Pouilly-Vinzelles also have a small number of premiers crus, from the 2024 vintage.

key: The Côte Chalonnaise is a broken line of hillsides, not a continuous escarpment; it has premiers crus but no grands crus.
Bouzeron is Aligoté only, Mercurey and Givry are mainly red, Rully more white, Montagny white only.
The Mâconnais is warmer; whites are Chardonnay and reds mostly Gamay. Mâcon-Villages is white only.
Pouilly-Fuissé covers Chaintré, Fuissé, Solutré-Pouilly and Vergisson, below the rocks of Solutré and Vergisson.
Pouilly-Fuissé gained 22 premiers crus in 2020, the first in the Mâconnais.

questions.q: Which Côte Chalonnaise village appellation is for white wine only?
questions.explain: Montagny is white only, from Chardonnay. Mercurey and Givry are mainly red, and Rully makes both.

questions.q: What does Mercurey mainly produce?
questions.explain: Mercurey, the largest village of the Côte Chalonnaise, makes mainly red Pinot Noir.

questions.q: In which year did Pouilly-Fuissé gain its premiers crus?
questions.explain: The 22 premiers crus of Pouilly-Fuissé were created in 2020, applying from the 2020 vintage.

questions.q: How many premiers crus does Pouilly-Fuissé have?
questions.explain: Pouilly-Fuissé has 22 premier cru climats.

questions.q: Which two limestone outcrops rise above Pouilly-Fuissé?
options: The hills of Corton and Montrachet
The Roche de Solutré and the Roche de Vergisson
The Montagne de Reims and the Côte des Blancs
questions.explain: The rocks of Solutré and Vergisson dominate the Pouilly-Fuissé landscape.

questions.q: Which grape makes most red wine in the Mâconnais?
questions.explain: Mâconnais reds are made mostly from Gamay.

questions.q: What colour is Mâcon-Villages?
questions.explain: Mâcon-Villages is an appellation for white wine only.

questions.q: How does the landscape of the Côte Chalonnaise differ from the Côte d'Or?
options: It is one longer and steeper continuous slope
It is a flat river plain
Its vineyards sit on scattered hillsides among other farmland
It is a high plateau of Portlandian limestone
questions.explain: The Côte Chalonnaise is not a continuous escarpment. Its vineyards are spread over separate hillsides.

questions.q: Which Côte Chalonnaise village appellation has no premiers crus?
questions.explain: Bouzeron, the Aligoté appellation, has no premiers crus. The other four villages do.

questions.q: Which is the largest village appellation of the Côte Chalonnaise?
questions.explain: Mercurey is the largest village and makes mainly red Pinot Noir.

questions.q: Which Côte Chalonnaise village makes more white than red and has a long sparkling wine history?
questions.explain: Rully makes more white than red and has long produced sparkling wine.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four communes of Pouilly-Fuissé?
questions.explain: Pouilly-Fuissé covers Chaintré, Fuissé, Solutré-Pouilly and Vergisson. Davayé gives its name to Mâcon Davayé.

questions.q: From which vintage do Pouilly-Loché and Pouilly-Vinzelles have premiers crus?
questions.explain: Their premiers crus apply from the 2024 vintage. Pouilly-Fuissé gained its premiers crus from 2020.

questions.q: What colour is Viré-Clessé?
questions.explain: Viré-Clessé is a village appellation for white wine from Chardonnay.

questions.q: Why are Mâconnais whites usually rounder and riper than those further north?
options: The Mâconnais is warmer and sunnier
They must be aged in new oak
questions.explain: The warmer, sunnier Mâconnais gives Chardonnay rounder, riper fruit.

questions.q: On which river does the town of Mâcon lie?
questions.explain: Mâcon lies on the Saône. The Serein is the river of Chablis.

cards.b: South of the Maranges, named after Chalon-sur-Saône. Vineyards lie on scattered hillsides, not one continuous slope.

cards.f: Does the Côte Chalonnaise have grands crus?
cards.b: No. Four of its five village appellations have premiers crus. Bouzeron has none.

cards.f: Name the five Côte Chalonnaise villages from north to south.
cards.b: Bouzeron, Rully, Mercurey, Givry and Montagny.
Village appellation for white wine from Aligoté only, promoted to village rank in 1998.
Makes more white than red and has a long history of sparkling wine production.
The largest village of the Côte Chalonnaise, making mainly red Pinot Noir.
Mainly red village. Tradition says it was a favourite of King Henri IV.
White only, from Chardonnay. A large part of it is classified as premier cru.

cards.f: How does the Mâconnais climate compare with the Côte d'Or?
cards.b: It is warmer and sunnier, so its Chardonnay is rounder and riper in fruit.

cards.f: Which grape makes most Mâconnais red?
cards.b: Gamay.
Mâconnais appellation for white wine only.

cards.f: What is Mâcon followed by a village name?
cards.b: A step above basic Mâcon, such as Mâcon Davayé or Mâcon Chardonnay.
Mâconnais village appellation for white wine from Chardonnay.
White wine appellation from Chardonnay in the south of the Mâconnais, recognised in 1971.

cards.f: Which four communes make up Pouilly-Fuissé?
cards.b: Chaintré, Fuissé, Solutré-Pouilly and Vergisson.

cards.f: Roche de Solutré and Roche de Vergisson
cards.b: Limestone outcrops that rise above the Pouilly-Fuissé vineyards.

cards.f: How does Pouilly-Fuissé differ from most Mâcon?
cards.b: It is white only, from Chardonnay, with more weight and structure, and is often aged in oak.
22 climats, created in 2020 and applying from the 2020 vintage. They were the first premiers crus of the Mâconnais.
Le Clos de Monsieur Noly, Les Crays, Vers Cras, Sur la Roche, Les Perrières, Le Clos Reyssier and Aux Quarts.

cards.f: Which premiers crus do Pouilly-Loché and Pouilly-Vinzelles have?
cards.b: From the 2024 vintage: Les Mûres in Loché, and Les Longeays, Les Pétaux and Les Quarts in Vinzelles.
